source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (AIJ 305)
finding: RBF-HS gives the same diagnoses as Reiter's HS-Tree, in the same best-first order, but in linear space. Memory drops a lot. Time usually stays close.
numbers: Minimum-cardinality setting: average memory factor saved 14.1 (ENT) and 13.8 (SPL), i.e. under 8% of HS-Tree memory; factor over 10 in 45% of cases, max 57 (SPL). Runtime above 1s in 94% of cases.
quote: RBF-HS ... saves substantial space while requiring only reasonably more or even less time than Reiter's HS-Tree
limits: Real-world ontology debugging problems; Pellet reasoner; sequential-diagnosis sessions averaged over 5 runs.
agent_relevance: Memory, not time, is what binds when we enumerate hypotheses. A forgetting search keeps all guarantees if re-exploration is cheap.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (AIJ 305)
finding: Surprise: forgetting and re-exploring is sometimes faster than remembering everything, because the open-node queue costs time.
numbers: Both lower runtime and large memory saving in 35% (ENT) and 38% (SPL) of cases. Worst RBF-HS time overhead factor 10.4 (SPL, ontology O).
limits: Explanation is the authors' own (priority-queue management cost); not isolated by an ablation.
agent_relevance: A bigger memory of hypotheses is not free. Pruned, re-derivable search may beat storing every open branch.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (AIJ 305)
finding: Failed condition: for most-probable (maxProb) diagnoses the trade is roughly one-to-one. RBF-HS does much worse when node scores differ only slightly.
numbers: maxProb: space-time tradeoff positive in 53% of cases; median 3.75x less space vs 3.56x more time (median 73% memory saved, HS-Tree 72% faster). minCard: avg space factor 18, max 158; time overhead below factor 2 in over 96% of scenarios, avg 1.2, max 2.7; both-better in 23%.
limits: Cause given: Korf's RBFS performs poorly when f-values are nearly equal ('mind shifts'). Applies to probability-ordered search.
agent_relevance: When scores are near-flat, depth-first re-exploration thrashes. Rank gaps matter for any linear-memory best-first loop.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (AIJ 305)
finding: Hybrid HBF-HS runs HS-Tree first, then switches to RBF-HS. It removes most of RBF-HS's time overhead and caps memory.
numbers: Switch at 400 nodes: median time overhead vs HS-Tree about 0% (ENT) and 3% (SPL); better than HS-Tree in 44% / 42% of cases; memory never above 416 nodes while HS-Tree needed over 500,000 (factor over 1000). Extra nodes after switch under 2% on average, max 4%. SPL,20 on ontology O: overhead 10.4 cut to 0.98.
limits: Switch threshold is hand-set. maxProb: HBF-HS usually comparable to HS-Tree, 43% better.
agent_relevance: Cheap breadth-first top, then bounded depth-first below. Fits a budgeted search schedule.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (AIJ 305)
finding: Hardest cases: ontology alignments with huge diagnoses (ccc, cce). HS-Tree runs out of memory; RBF-HS finishes.
numbers: ccc,ENT,2: HS-Tree used over 800x the memory, RBF-HS 3% faster. ccc,SPL,6: over 4200x less memory, 15% less time. ccc,SPL,20: 99.9% memory reduction, 65% time saving. cce,ENT: HS-Tree out of memory in 3 of 5 runs (under 3 min); RBF-HS avg 2.5 min with at most 102 nodes. cce,SPL,20: HS-Tree out of memory after 37 min; RBF-HS under 11 min, 125 nodes.
limits: Only two ontology pairs; benefit grows with problem hardness.
agent_relevance: Gains concentrate on hard instances; a scaffold should not judge an algorithm on easy ones.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (AIJ 305)
finding: Boundary: when every diagnosis has cardinality one, trees are tiny and HS-Tree can use less memory than RBF-HS.
numbers: 5 scenarios (ontologies K and C) had HS-Tree using slightly less memory. Scalability: ld=100 fine for minCard; for maxProb RBF-HS took up to several hours per session while HS-Tree and HBF-HS (60% memory switch) took minutes.
limits: Depth-first can need more space than breadth-first on shallow trees.
agent_relevance: Do not use the heavy method on shallow, easy problems.

source: Rodler (2023) Memory-Limited Model-Based Diagnosis (IJCAI-23 journal-track abstract)
finding: The IJCAI 2023 item is Rodler's extended abstract of RBF-HS, not a Jannach et al. paper. It repeats the headline results on 12 knowledge-base diagnosis problems.
numbers: Average / max memory saving 93% / 98%; both lower time and lower space in 38% of cases; one case 85% runtime and 98% memory saving; HS-Tree ran out of 32 GB in several cases while RBF-HS solved them. k in {2,6,10,20}, Pellet.
quote: RBF-HS is applicable to any hitting-set problem, and thus has the potential to positively impact a number of important domains
limits: Extended abstract; full numbers are in the AIJ paper. Source attribution in the subfield row needs correcting.
agent_relevance: Flag: SUBFIELDS.md row credits Jannach et al.; the opened source is by Rodler alone.

source: Rodler (2022) Sound, Complete, Linear-Space, Best-First Diagnosis Search (arXiv 2009.12190, DX-2020 version)
finding: Short version with 12 ontology problems of 42 to 33,203 axioms, from expressivity ALCON to SROIQ. Reports absolute run size too.
numbers: Absolute runtime min/avg/max 0.04 / 24 / 744 s; space 9 / 17.5K / 1.3M tree nodes. Memory overhead of HS-Tree reached 4900% (factor up to 50). 40% of cases had RBF-HS time lower or equal; best saving over 88% time (case D,20).
limits: Fewer scenarios than AIJ; same author. No independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Absolute numbers show the tasks are small enough that memory, not hours of time, is the issue.

source: Rodler (2020) DynamicHS: Streamlining Reiter's Hitting-Set Tree for Sequential Diagnosis
finding: Keeping the HS-tree between diagnosis iterations (instead of rebuilding) saves time. This answers a question Reiter posed in 1987.
numbers: Faster than HS-Tree in 99.4% of scenarios and 96% of sessions; median saving 52%, max 75%; hardest cases median 64%, max 89%; in single sessions HS-Tree took over 9x as long. Heuristics ENT / SPL / MPS median savings about 50 / 52 / 52%, no significant difference (ANOVA p=0.26).
quote: DynamicHS required less time than HS-Tree in 96 % of the executed sequential diagnosis sessions.
limits: Trades time for space (statefulness). A few scenarios HS-Tree won: up to 86% faster in one case, 76% in another. Same author and same corpus as RBF-HS.
agent_relevance: Reuse of earlier search state across steps pays about half the time. Mirrors keeping hypotheses alive between turns.

source: Shchekotykhin, Jannach, Schmitz (2015) MergeXplain: Fast Computation of Multiple Conflicts for Diagnosis (IJCAI)
finding: Finding several conflicts per call (divide and merge, instead of QuickXplain's one) speeds up hitting-set diagnosis. Gain is larger when the checks are costly and problems bigger.
numbers: DXC circuits, finding 5 diagnoses: avg improvement 25% (full conflict mode) and 37% (aggressive mode); c432 45% and 47%; 74181 29% and 32%. CSP benchmarks up to 54% (costasArray-13: 1,379,842 ms vs 629,366 ms). Simulated: 20-30% in the random case, up to 75% in unfavourable cases.
quote: MERGEXPLAIN can help to significantly reduce the required computation times
limits: Can lose: queens-8 -11%, revenue calculation -5%, and slight degradation when only one conflict exists. Parallelising MergeXplain rarely helped on DXC/CSP because checks under 1 ms.
agent_relevance: Ask a conflict finder for many minimal conflicts per call. Savings depend on cost per check.

source: Jannach, Schmitz, Shchekotykhin (2016) Parallelized Hitting Set Computation for Model-Based Diagnosis (AAAI 2015 / extended)
finding: Parallel HS-tree expansion on a 4-thread pool beats the sequential version, with no diagnoses lost.
numbers: Significant (p<=0.05) in 96 of 100 DXC scenarios; speedups 1.78 to 3.44 (over 70% less time). Simulated checks: speedup above 3 once check time reaches 1 ms; 8 threads up to 7.27 (over 85% reduction) for larger conflicts.
limits: With zero-cost checks gains are modest (thread overhead). Redundant conflict computations still occur. Full parallel not always better than level-wise.
agent_relevance: Parallel workers help only when each check is slow; LLM calls are slow, so parallel branch checks are plausible.

source: Felfernig, Schubert, Zehentner (2012/2021) An Efficient Diagnosis Algorithm for Inconsistent Constraint Sets (FastDiag, arXiv 2102.09005)
finding: FastDiag finds one minimal diagnosis directly with about the effort of one conflict (log2 consistency checks), skipping conflicts and hitting sets. It beats HSDAG for leading diagnoses.
numbers: Bicycle CLib configuration (34 variables, about 65 constraints). Complexity about log2(n/k)+2k checks. Prediction RMSD: FastDiag 0.95, best-first HSDAG 0.97, breadth-first HSDAG 1.64. Mann-Whitney: best-first vs breadth-first p=6.625e-5.
limits: Small benchmark, 2GB desktop; speed shown mostly in figures. Pays off for first-n diagnoses, not full enumeration.
agent_relevance: For 'give me one good fix fast', a direct method beats building the full conflict-hitting structure.

source: Shchekotykhin, Fleiss, Rodler, Friedrich (2012) Direct computation of diagnoses for ontology debugging (arXiv 1209.0997)
finding: Computing diagnoses without first computing conflicts (inverse QuickXplain and inverse HS-tree) works on aligned ontologies where standard HS-Tree fails.
numbers: 146 OAEI-2011 ontology alignments; both methods succeed on 133. 13 ontologies only diagnosable with the direct method (HS-Tree stuck within 2 hours, e.g. 1 diagnosis for csa-conference-ekaw). With 1 diagnosis requested the direct approach is faster. Query-discrimination timings are mixed: LogMap SPL 6.6 vs 15.1 s, but MapSSS ENT 81.1 vs 56.2 s.
limits: Direct approach not uniformly faster; advantage shrinks as more diagnoses are requested.
agent_relevance: When conflicts are many, skip conflict enumeration and go straight to repairs.

source: Ignatiev, Morgado, Marques-Silva (2017) Model Based Diagnosis of Multiple Observations with Implicit Hitting Sets (arXiv 1707.01972)
finding: Handling many failing observations at once via implicit hitting sets scales; analysing observations separately does not.
numbers: 1140 'buggy encoder' CNF instances: IHS solves all, largest about 0.1 s. Separate enumeration with LBX / RS completes only 177 / 185 instances (only k<8). Aggregated formula grows to millions of variables and clauses while the IHS formula stays at thousands.
limits: Synthetic family built by the authors to show the effect; MaxSAT/SAT oracle, not description logics.
agent_relevance: Pool the evidence of several failing cases instead of diagnosing each alone.

source: MergeXplain related work: Satoh & Uno 2005; Stern et al. 2012; Liffiton et al. 2015 (dual-problem diagnosis), as cited
finding: The related-work section groups speedups of Reiter's method: exploit structure (hierarchy, distribution), parallelise, solve the dual problem, or use approximate stochastic / greedy search.
numbers: Not numeric. MergeXplain itself leaves the HS-tree procedure unchanged and makes no assumption about problem structure.
limits: Second-hand description of cited works; those papers themselves were not opened.
agent_relevance: Map of the efficiency family: structure, parallelism, duality, approximation, memory.

source: MergeXplain footnote 2: HS-tree versus direct encodings
finding: Direct encodings (e.g. MaxSAT) are typically more efficient than HS-tree when only ONE diagnosis is needed; HS-tree is favourable when several diagnoses and a black-box reasoner are required.
numbers: Qualitative; no figure given.
limits: Authors' remark, not a test. MaxSAT-based results by Ignatiev et al. support it for minimum-size diagnoses.
agent_relevance: Choose the algorithm by the question: one fix versus a ranked set of explanations.

source: Rodler AIJ 2022: same algorithm under minCard vs maxProb
finding: The same algorithm behaves very differently under two preference criteria, so one benchmark result does not transfer to the other criterion.
numbers: minCard: positive tradeoff in 94-96% of scenarios. maxProb: 53% positive, median factors 3.75 vs 3.56. ld=100 maxProb: RBF-HS hours vs minutes.
limits: Authors tested only these two orderings.
agent_relevance: Check the ranking signal before trusting a method that was tuned on another one.

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets (QXR)
finding: Opened LLM study that uses QuickXplain and a hitting set. An LLM is a noisy consistency oracle; localise minimal conflicting claim subsets, then delete a small hitting set. It beats asking the LLM once to fix the whole set.
numbers: VitaminC recall (direct to QXR): Sonnet 4.5 0.617 to 0.957; Opus 4.6 0.574 to 0.968; Sonnet 3.7 0.854 to 0.975; Mistral Large 2 0.603 to 0.978; DeepSeek-R1 0.730 to 0.990. Clusters 24-32 claims, 2-6 injected contradictions. Single oracle call per query, temperature 0.
limits: Gain smaller on FEVER (Opus 4.6 direct F1 0.989 vs QXR 0.964, so QXR lost); Sonnet 4.5 precision dropped 0.997 to 0.975 on VitaminC. Synthetic injected conflicts. Authors' own work; not replicated.
agent_relevance: Closest direct evidence for our agent: conflict localisation then minimal repair beats one-shot judging.

source: He et al. (2026) QXR, RAMDocs RAG results
finding: On RAG snippets with conflicting evidence the same pattern holds, and weaker models gain most.
numbers: RAMDocs, N=30 claims, 10 gold conflicts: Qwen2.5 7B F1 0.741 to 0.815 (R 0.639 to 0.743); Qwen2.5 32B 0.845 to 0.920 (R 0.839 to 0.998); Haiku 4.5 0.724 to 0.863 (R 0.575 to 0.810); Sonnet 4.5 0.882 to 0.870 (no gain, precision 0.962 to 0.887); DeepSeek-V4-Pro 0.861 to 0.904.
limits: Strongest model gained nothing on F1. Chain-of-thought, decomposition, few-shot and self-consistency prompts did not remove over-pruning for direct judging (their Section F, reported by authors, not opened in detail).
agent_relevance: Structure helps weaker or over-cautious judges; benefit is small where one-shot judging is already good.

source: He et al. (2026) QXR, cost analysis
finding: Cost is the price: many LLM calls. Query count is O(I*m*k*log N).
numbers: 435 oracle calls at N=30 claims and 4,950 at N=100 (quoted). Uncached token cost at most O(Q) times a single full-set judgment, though localisation queries are shorter.
limits: No majority voting used. Early stop and sampling of scopes proposed but not tested.
agent_relevance: Budget this: conflict localisation with an LLM oracle is call-hungry; the efficient-algorithm literature (MergeXplain, FastDiag) targets exactly this.

source: He et al. (2026) QXR, theory notes
finding: Minimum-deletion repair equals a hitting set over all MUSes (NP-hard). QXR uses greedy hitting set with a proved approximation lemma. Naive divide and conquer fails when a conflict crosses the split.
numbers: Theory: deleting a hitting set of discovered MUSes yields a consistent set; one crossing MUS breaks independent halves.
limits: Guarantees assume a perfect judge; the LLM is noisy.
agent_relevance: Reiter's hitting-set theorem carries over to claim sets judged by an LLM.

source: Zhu & Chang (2026) A Verifier Can Leak the Answer: Diagnosability Before Optimization in Closed-Loop Agent Debugging
finding: Agent-debugging study where exact minimum hitting set and a greedy method gave identical results, because the verifier already encoded the target. A better solver then proves nothing.
numbers: Exact MHS and greedy: identical supports in 12/12 dev cases, same planted-fault recovery in 9/12. Exact-anchor predicates gave the planted pair in 9/9; after removing anchors recovery 8/9. Heldout 1,440 cases: 55/72 units passed reference gate, 54/55 runtime gate; false admission 0/20 (95% upper bound 0.1391).
quote: The optimizer was correct, but the verifier had already disclosed the answer.
limits: Small dev set (12), one closed-loop decision agent, preprint, authors' own.
agent_relevance: Warning for our evaluation: check that the test does not reveal the answer before comparing diagnosis algorithms.

source: Rodler AIJ 2022: preservation of guarantees
finding: All reported savings come with identical output: RBF-HS, HBF-HS and HS-Tree return the same diagnoses; no completeness or soundness is traded.
numbers: Same diagnoses by proof (footnote 6 of the DX version). Needs a fixed finite number ld of diagnoses (ld in 2, 6, 10, 20; scalability 100).
limits: Linear space applies to enumerating a fixed count, not an unbounded stream.
agent_relevance: Efficiency without losing completeness is possible, but only for a bounded K of hypotheses.

source: Rodler DynamicHS: boundary cases
finding: DynamicHS has no win in a handful of scenarios and uses more memory. Slight losses in median runtime were seen.
numbers: Median losses of -2% (SPL, D, 30) and -3% (MPS, fal-ce, 30); single hardest-case losses up to 86% and 76% (HS-Tree faster).
limits: Memory increase 'reasonable in the vast majority' of scenarios, not all.
agent_relevance: Stateful reuse is not free; report where it loses.

source: MergeXplain simulated study: conflict position
finding: QuickXplain performance depends strongly on where conflicts sit in the input. MergeXplain's gain is largest in unlucky layouts.
numbers: Random layout 20-30% gain; clustered layouts up to 75% (100 components, 2 conflicts of size 5, LaR: 75%); negative in some cells (-8%, -4%).
limits: Generated problems with simulated check times capped at 10 ms; not real reasoners.
agent_relevance: Input ordering can dominate cost in a divide-and-conquer conflict finder; shuffle or order by likelihood.

source: Jannach et al. parallel HS-tree: problem characteristics
finding: Gains depend on conflict size, check time and problem structure. More components lowers relative gain; larger conflicts raise it.
numbers: Statistically significant in all CSP/spreadsheet tests; some reductions over 50%, others modest.
limits: Overhead of thread creation hurts if checks are under about 1 ms.
agent_relevance: Parallelise only costly checks.

source: Direct ontology debugging vs HS-Tree, time table
finding: Mixed timing evidence between direct and conflict-based methods on discrimination tasks; no clear winner across matchers.
numbers: Per-matcher times (INV-HS-TREE vs HS-TREE): AgrMaker SPL 36.04 vs 36.03; GOMMA-bk ENT 18.34 vs 14.47; Lily SPL 82.9 vs 115.2; LogMap ENT 6.60 vs 13.41.
limits: Only 7 matchers; times in seconds; no significance tests reported.
agent_relevance: Prefer the direct method for coverage on hard cases, not for speed in general.

source: FastDiag precision analysis
finding: On predicting which diagnosis a user will pick, FastDiag and best-first HSDAG have the best precision; breadth-first HSDAG is worst.
numbers: RMSD 0.95 / 0.97 / 1.64 (FastDiag / best-first / breadth-first).
limits: Single configuration knowledge base; user choices simulated.
agent_relevance: Preference ordering matters as much as speed.
